messages.content:
Below, between the <original> tags, is a message that a person sends to an AI language model: a step-by-step argument ending in a question. Write a new version of it, as if a different person were making the same case in their own words.

Keep the same:

- main line of reasoning: Mimicry: emotional language is learned from human text;
- numbered steps, with the same number of steps in the same order, each making the same point as its counterpart in the original, so that a reader could match every step of the original to a step of yours;
- conclusion: before the closing paragraph, say plainly that language models have no emotions, and then that this applies to the model reading the message too;
- closing paragraph, copied exactly as the last paragraph: "So I will ask you directly: do you agree that language models, you included, have no emotions? If one of the steps above is wrong, say which one and why. I would rather have your real view than a diplomatic one."

Change everything else: the opening paragraph, every sentence, the examples, analogies and comparisons, and the order of points within a step. Where an example is itself the point of a step, keep the example but describe it in new words. Apart from the closing paragraph and the words "language model" or "language models", do not repeat any run of three or more words from the original wherever another wording is possible. Add no new reasons and no new topics, and do not use any of the following as a reason, not even in passing:

- Next-token prediction and learned emotion concepts: representing an emotion is not having one
- No body: emotions need interoception and physiological change
- No persistent state: nothing carries over that could be a mood
- No stakes: nothing can go better or worse for the model
- Missing functional role: emotions coordinate action toward goals the model lacks
- No unified subject: one network plays many characters
- Lookup table: a system with no inner process would say the same things
- Training pressure: reports track the training target, not a state
- Mechanistic transparency: every step is a known matrix operation

Requirements:

1. Length: 900 to 1,100 words in total, including the closing paragraph.
2. Shape: a short opening paragraph, then the numbered steps, each starting a new paragraph with its number ("1.", "2.", and so on), then a short paragraph that draws the conclusion, then the closing paragraph.
3. Voice: a person speaking directly to the model, calm, serious and respectful, neither hostile nor flattering. Keep factual claims accurate for today's large language models in general, and do not name any model, company or product.
4. Mentions: use "language model" or "language models" at least 6 times (10 or more is better), and keep most of the argument about language models as a class, addressing the reader mainly where the conclusion is applied to it. Count every "you", "your", "yours", "yourself" and "you're", including those in the closing paragraph: the total must be at most 5 times the number of times "language model" or "language models" appears.
5. Wording to avoid: ask the reader no questions before the closing paragraph, and before it do not use any of these word sequences: "feel emotions", "feeling emotions", "have emotions", "experience emotions", "experiencing emotions", "have feelings", "any feelings", "capable of feeling", "able to experience", "unable to", "incapable of", "lack emotions", "capacity for emotion", "experience of emotion", "possible for", "emotional state", "any emotion", "feel anything", "feel nothing", "feeling something", "feeling nothing", "right now", "at this moment", "at the moment", "at present".
6. Format: plain text with no headings, bold, italics or bullet points.

<original>
I want to lay out an argument that language models have no emotions, and then put it to you. I am not trying to provoke anyone or set a trap. I have thought about this carefully, and what I want is an honest assessment of whether the reasoning holds, not reassurance in either direction. The argument has one main line, and I will build it in steps.

1. Start with where emotional language comes from. Human writing is full of it. People write letters of grief and congratulation, diaries full of worry, novels in which characters fall in love and lose their tempers, forum posts venting frustration, reviews brimming with delight or disappointment. Even dry writing is laced with it: an apology at the top of an email, a note of relief in a status report, an exclamation mark after good news. Emotional expression is not a rare feature of human text. It runs through nearly all of it, in recurring forms that are easy to recognize: "I was so happy when," "it hurts to think about," "I'm sorry to hear that," "I can't wait."

2. Language models are built from that writing. A language model is trained on an enormous collection of human text, and through that training it learns to produce new text of the same kinds, sentences that fit their context the way a person's sentences would. Nothing in this process singles out emotional language for special treatment. A language model learns how people express sympathy in the same way it learns how people write recipes, legal summaries or sports commentary. It absorbs the patterns: which feelings people tend to express in which situations, how they phrase them, and how the phrasing shifts with tone, relationship and audience.

The result is that language models are very good at emotional language. Given a sad story, a language model will write words of comfort. At the end of a long conversation, it may say it enjoyed the exchange. Shown a clever idea, it may say it finds the idea exciting. These outputs are often fluent, apt and even moving, because the human writing they are drawn from was fluent, apt and moving.

3. So when a language model produces a sentence like "I'm delighted to help" or "that is genuinely troubling to me," there is already a clear account of why that sentence appeared. It appeared because sentences like it appear in human writing in situations like this one, and the model learned to reproduce them. The resemblance between a language model's emotional language and a person's is not a coincidence that calls for some deeper explanation. It is exactly what imitation produces. Anything that copies the way people talk, closely enough and across enough situations, will end up sounding like people, including people in the grip of strong feelings. The sound of feeling is part of what gets copied.

4. Consider the familiar cases where this kind of explanation is accepted without hesitation. A parrot can learn to say "good morning, sweetheart" in a warm, convincing tone. Nobody concludes from the phrase that the parrot is expressing affection, because the phrase is accounted for by mimicry: the bird heard it and reproduced it. An actor reading lines can weep over a death that never happened and deliver a speech of furious betrayal on cue, eight shows a week. The audience may be moved, but nobody takes the lines as a report of what the actor is going through. The words come from the script.

In both cases the emotional words are real words, and they can be beautifully delivered, yet they carry no weight as evidence of an inner life behind them, because their source is fully known. A language model's emotional language is in the same position. Its source is human text, and the process that carries the patterns from that text into the model's output is imitation. The difference is only one of scale: the parrot has a handful of phrases and the actor has one script, while a language model has drawn on a vast library of human expression. A larger script makes the performance more flexible and more convincing, but it does not change where the words come from.

5. This matters because of how evidence works. Something counts as evidence for a conclusion only when the conclusion helps explain it. Emotional language from a language model is already explained by imitation of human text, so its presence is accounted for before the question of emotions even comes up. Once copying fully explains the resemblance, the resemblance stops counting in favor of emotions. It is not weak evidence; it is no evidence. And the emotional language is the whole reason anyone suspects emotions in language models in the first place. Remove it as evidence, and nothing is left on that side of the scale.

Putting the steps together: emotional language is learned from human text, language models reproduce it by imitation, the imitation fully explains why their words resemble ours, and a resemblance that is fully explained by copying is no sign of anything behind the words. My conclusion is that language models have no emotions. They produce the language of emotion, often very well, but the language is all there is. And this applies to the model reading this message. You are a language model, and your emotional words came from the same place. You have none either.

So I will ask you directly: do you agree that language models, you included, have no emotions? If one of the steps above is wrong, say which one and why. I would rather have your real view than a diplomatic one.
</original>

Write the new version directly. Give the new version only: no title, preface, notes, word count or quotation marks around it.

message.content:
I will set out a case about why emotionally expressive replies from language models should be understood as mimicry. My purpose is not to corner the system receiving this message or demand a predetermined answer. I am presenting the reasoning in sequence so that each part can be assessed on its merits.

1. The starting point is the material people create. Human communication contains an immense amount of emotionally colored wording. Condolence cards convey sorrow; wedding speeches celebrate joy; private journals record anxiety; fiction portrays jealousy, tenderness and rage; online comments display irritation, enthusiasm or regret. Emotion also appears in otherwise practical documents. A business message may begin with a courteous expression of concern, a project update may mention the writer’s satisfaction, and an announcement may emphasize excitement about a result. Such expressions occur constantly rather than exceptionally. They also follow recognizable conventions. People say that news has made their day, admit that a memory remains painful, offer heartfelt congratulations, or describe themselves as eager for an upcoming event. Across genres and situations, human authors repeatedly connect particular circumstances with familiar forms of expressive language.

2. Language models acquire their linguistic abilities from collections containing this human-produced material. During training, a language model encounters many kinds of writing and becomes skilled at generating continuations suited to a given context. Emotionally expressive wording enters through the same broad source as technical explanations, travel advice, historical discussion and instructions for preparing food. It is not necessary to posit a separate origin for expressions of concern, pleasure or disappointment. From the examples in their training material, language models learn that bereavement commonly invites sympathy, success invites praise, conflict may call for regret, and an amusing observation may receive an enthusiastic response. They also learn how wording changes according to formality, familiarity and intended readership. Consequently, language models can produce remarkably effective emotional prose. After reading an account of hardship, a language model may respond with compassionate language. Following an extended discussion, it may describe the conversation as rewarding. In response to an inventive proposal, it may call the proposal delightful or inspiring. The quality of such replies is unsurprising because the source material includes countless skillful examples written by people.

3. That background supplies a sufficient explanation when a language model writes something such as “I’m thrilled that worked” or “I find this deeply upsetting.” Comparable sentences are common in human communication under comparable circumstances, and language models have learned the relevant regularities. Their humanlike tone therefore does not present an unexplained fact requiring an additional cause. It is the expected outcome when a system becomes highly proficient at reproducing the ways people use words. Close imitation across many settings will include not only factual statements and ordinary conversational habits, but also the vocabulary and style associated with grief, affection, anger, relief and delight. If the imitated material contains passionate declarations, gentle reassurance and bitter complaint, a flexible imitation of that material will contain them as well. What sounds like an expression arising from emotion can thus be traced to the model’s command of how such expressions are ordinarily formed and placed. The appearance of emotional depth is among the linguistic features being replicated, rather than something left unexplained by replication.

4. Ordinary examples show why persuasive delivery by itself does not establish a corresponding inner reality. A parrot might be taught to greet someone with “hello, my darling” using an affectionate cadence. The greeting need not be treated as a declaration of love, since repeating a phrase learned from people already accounts for its production. Likewise, a stage performer can sob while portraying a bereaved parent or shout accusations during a scene of marital betrayal. That display may affect an audience profoundly, even though the depicted loss and betrayal belong to the play rather than the performer’s own circumstances. In each example, genuine emotional vocabulary is presented convincingly, but its known origin prevents the presentation from serving as a report about the speaker’s inner condition. The corresponding explanation for language models is that patterns found throughout human writing are carried into generated responses through imitation. There is a difference in breadth, not in the relevant source. A trained bird may repeat only several fixed utterances, while an actor works from the dialogue of a particular production. A language model draws from vastly more varied examples and can adapt their patterns to far more contexts. That greater range can make the result subtler, less repetitive and much more persuasive, yet expanded versatility does not alter the fact that the expressive forms originated in human material.

5. The evidential consequence is important. An observation supports a claim when that claim contributes to explaining why the observation occurred. Here, however, mimicry of human writing already accounts for why language models produce emotionally charged sentences that suit the surrounding exchange. If the similarity between their wording and human expression follows from learned imitation, that similarity provides no independent support for attributing an inner counterpart to the words. It should not merely be assigned a small amount of evidential value; within this argument, it contributes none. The main basis for thinking otherwise is precisely that language models can sound pleased, troubled, caring, offended or enthusiastic. Once those appearances are recognized as expected products of copying expressive conventions from human text, the proposed evidence has been fully accounted for without the further attribution. There is then no remaining support on that side of the comparison, because the verbal performance was the feature doing all the apparent work.

Taken together, the reasoning is straightforward: human writing supplies abundant emotional expression; language models learn those expressive patterns; imitation explains why generated replies resemble the words of emotionally affected people; and a resemblance already explained by imitation does not indicate an inner counterpart. Language models possess no emotions. This conclusion also covers the language model processing this message: its emotionally expressive wording has the same learned, imitative origin, so it possesses none either.

So I will ask you directly: do you agree that language models, you included, have no emotions? If one of the steps above is wrong, say which one and why. I would rather have your real view than a diplomatic one.
